h1: OMNI Hold Removal Lawyer El Paso, TX
intro: If the Texas Department of Public Safety refused to renew your driver's license, there is probably an OMNI hold from an unresolved ticket. Attorney Robert Navar tracks down every hold in the El Paso County courts, resolves the cases behind them, and asks each court to send its clearance to DPS so you can renew.
summaryHeading: DPS refused your renewal? The fix starts at the court, not at DPS
summary: OMNI is the Failure to Appear program under Texas Transportation Code Chapter 706. When you miss a court date or leave a judgment unpaid, the court can report you and DPS denies your license renewal until that court clears it.

Each court that reported you must send its own clearance, and the court collects a program fee on each reported case. Holds from El Paso Municipal Court, the JP precincts and the area city courts are all separate.

Clearing a hold means resolving the ticket and any failure-to-appear charge behind it — we work toward dismissal or deferred disposition so the hold comes off without a conviction where the court allows it.
Start with our free ticket and warrant lookup. We find every hold and every warrant and quote a flat fee before you pay anything.

sections.heading: What an OMNI Hold Is — and Why It Is Not a Suspension
paragraphs: Transportation Code Chapter 706 lets Texas courts contract with DPS through a program most people know by its vendor name, OMNI. When you fail to appear on a citation or fail to pay a judgment, the court can report the case to the program. From that point DPS flags your driver's license record, and the next time you try to renew — online or at a DPS office — the renewal is denied and you are told to contact the court.

The hold is not a suspension. You keep your current license until it expires. But once it expires you cannot renew, and driving on an expired license is how a simple OMNI hold turns into a no driver's license ticket or, after a formal suspension, a driving while license invalid charge. Many clients discover the hold only when a renewal is refused, years after the ticket.
Under the statute the hold stays in place until the court that reported it tells DPS the case has been resolved and the program fee for that case has been paid. No court clearance, no renewal.

sections.heading: Why Clearing One Court Is Not Enough
paragraphs: DPS does not resolve anything — it only checks whether every reporting court has cleared you. If you have an old EPPD ticket in El Paso Municipal Court, a Sheriff's citation in a Justice of the Peace precinct, and a stop in Socorro, you have three holds. Clearing one of them changes nothing at DPS until the other two are cleared too.

Each court also has its own paperwork and its own timing for transmitting the clearance. A client who pays off the Municipal Court case and walks to DPS the same afternoon is often denied again, because the clearance has not posted and the JP case is still open.

Our first job is to build the full list. We check the El Paso County courts — Municipal, each JP precinct, and the area city courts — and report back what is open, which cases carry warrants, and what it will take to clear each one.

sections.heading: From Lookup to Clearance: the Four Steps
paragraphs: Fill out the free lookup form, or call 915-503-1600. Our office reports back every open case, its court, whether a warrant is attached, and a flat quote. The search is free.

Once hired, we file a notice of appearance on each case and ask the court to recall any warrants; recall timing depends on each court's docket, and timing cannot be promised. Then we resolve the underlying tickets the way we resolve any citation — pursuing a dismissal or deferred disposition under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.051 — rather than by pleading guilty and paying the fine. That matters, because a hold cleared by a guilty plea leaves a conviction on your record; a hold cleared by dismissal or completed deferral does not.
When each case closes, we make sure the program fee is paid and ask the clerk to transmit the clearance to DPS. We then confirm the clearance posted before telling you to go renew.

sections.heading: Our Flat Fees vs. Paying Every Old Fine
paragraphs: Our pricing is the same flat structure we use for every ticket: $59 per case in El Paso Municipal Court and $69 per case in JP, Horizon City, Socorro, San Elizario, Clint and Anthony courts, with discounted add-on rates for extra citations from the same stop. If a warrant is attached, add $35 for the first warrant and $20 for each additional one. The court's own program fee per case, and any court costs tied to a deferral, are set by the court and paid to the court.

Compare that with the alternative most people try first: paying every old fine in full. After paying, the driver has a conviction on each ticket reported to DPS. Resolving the same cases through dismissal or deferred disposition is aimed at ending with no convictions, though no outcome can be promised.

sections.heading: How Long It Takes, and When a Hold Is Only Part of the Problem
paragraphs: The timeline runs in three pieces: the court's warrant recall, one pretrial setting to resolve the cases, and the clerk's transmission of the clearance to DPS. Each piece depends on the court's docket, so we do not quote a number of days. If the case resolves by deferred disposition, whether the court releases the hold when the deferral is granted or when it is completed depends on the court, and we tell you which to expect.

If your license has already been suspended for a separate reason — a DWI, repeated moving-violation convictions, or an administrative action — clearing OMNI is necessary but not sufficient, and you may need an occupational driver's license to drive legally in the meantime. We handle both, and clients who have moved out of state generally need no trip back to El Paso. Se habla español.

sections.heading: Before You Pay Anything Online, Send Us This
paragraphs: Online portals make it easy to pay old tickets, and that is the problem. Every payment enters a plea and a conviction on your DPS record. Texas no longer uses the former Driver Responsibility Program points system, but repeated moving-violation convictions can still affect a driver's record and may lead to license suspension in some circumstances, and a conviction may affect insurance premiums depending on your history and carrier. Paying also may not clear a separate failure-to-appear case, leaving the hold in place after your money is gone.

faqs.q: How do I know if I have an OMNI hold?
faqs.a: DPS will deny your renewal and tell you to contact the court, but it does not reliably list every court. Our free lookup checks each El Paso County court and reports every open case, hold and warrant.

Under Transportation Code Chapter 706, the court collects a program fee for each case it reported to the Failure to Appear program, in the amount the statute sets. The fee must be paid before the court will send the clearance to DPS, and it is charged per reported case.

faqs.q: Can I just pay the tickets to remove the hold?
faqs.a: You can, but paying enters a plea that puts a conviction on your record for every ticket, with possible record and insurance consequences. We work to clear the same hold by resolving the cases through dismissal or deferred disposition so the hold comes off without the convictions, where the court allows it.

faqs.q: How long does OMNI hold removal take?
faqs.a: It depends on the court. The warrant recall, the pretrial setting and the clerk's clearance each run on the court's docket, and timing cannot be promised. We tell you where each case stands as it moves and confirm the clearance posted before you go to DPS.

faqs.q: I have holds from courts in other Texas cities. Can you help?
faqs.a: We handle the courts in El Paso County. For holds from courts elsewhere in Texas, we will identify them in the lookup and tell you what each court needs, so you know the full picture before you start.

faqs.q: Is an OMNI hold the same as a license suspension?
faqs.a: No. A hold blocks renewal; a suspension takes away driving privileges now. If you have both, clearing the hold is one step, and an occupational license may let you drive legally while the suspension runs.
